title: Control-Flow Graphs, Strings, and Arrays
summary: This unit covers control-flow graphs (Kontrollflussgraphen) as a representation of program executions and the reducibility (Reduzierbarkeit) of control flow. It also covers variable initialization (Variableninitialisierung), string concatenation (String-Konkatenation) and comparison, one- and two-dimensional arrays, and for-loops (For-Schleifen) and their equivalence to while-loops.
keyFacts: A path from Start to Stop corresponds to an execution; together with the state carried along it, it describes the operational semantics.
A condition node has exactly one yes edge and one no edge.
For an if statement, the body edge leads to the next statement; for a while loop, it leads back to the condition.
Every MiniJava program has a CFG; conversely, a CFG can be converted into a structured program if and only if it is reducible.
A reducible graph has exactly one entry point for each loop.
Local variables have no default value; reading one before its first assignment is a compiler error.
In string concatenation with +, the other operand is converted to text, and evaluation proceeds from left to right.
s1.equals(s2) compares string contents; == does not compare the text.
An array has a fixed length and contains values of the same type; for length n, the valid indices are 0 through n-1.
The elements of a newly created int array are initialized to 0; a length of 0 is allowed.
An array variable stores a reference; an assignment such as b = a does not create a new array.
A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays; its rows may have different lengths.
In a for loop, the update runs after the body and before the next condition check.
The for loop for(init; cond; upd) is equivalent to init followed by a while loop whose body first executes the original body and then the update.

review.notes: Alle 44 Fragen geprüft. Korrigiert wurden ein For-Schleifen-Distraktor samt Erklärung sowie die missverständlich formulierte Grammatik-Frage; deren Quelle wurde passend auf die For-Schleife gesetzt. Keine Frage musste entfernt oder ersetzt werden.

questions.prompt: In a control-flow graph (CFG), what does a path from Start to Stop correspond to?

options.text: A possible execution of the program

questions.explanation: A Start-to-Stop path describes a possible execution. The specific edges taken at branches depend on the current variable values.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about nodes and edges in a CFG. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A condition node has exactly one no edge.
The Start node must have an incoming edge.
A condition node has exactly one yes edge.
Every node except Stop has exactly two outgoing edges.
Every node except Start has incoming edges.

questions.explanation: Conditions branch into exactly yes and no. In addition, every node except Start has an incoming edge; Start therefore needs no incoming edge.

questions.prompt: In a `while` loop, the edge after the loop body leads back to the condition.
questions.explanation: This is the key control-flow difference from an `if`: after the body, the condition is checked again in a `while` loop.

questions.prompt: Local variables have no default value. Reading one before assigning it results in a ___.
questions.explanation: A local variable must be defined before it is used. Otherwise, the compiler reports `variable n might not have been initialized`.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a string literal such as `"Hello"`?

options.text: A string literal is always empty.
The quotation marks delimit the text but are not part of it.
The quotation marks are part of the stored text.
A string literal may contain only digits.

questions.explanation: The quotation marks delimit the string in the program. The stored text is just `Hello`.

questions.prompt: Which method compares the contents of strings?
questions.explanation: `equals` compares string contents. In this lecture, `==` is explicitly not the way to compare text.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an array is correct?

options.text: It can be created only at compile time.
It contains a fixed number of values of the same type.
It contains values of arbitrary types and has a variable length.

questions.explanation: An array has a fixed length and stores values of the same type. Its length can be determined at runtime, but remains fixed afterward.

questions.prompt: For an array of length $n$, the valid indices are ___.
questions.explanation: Arrays start at index 0 and end at `n-1`. Accessing `a[n]` is already outside the array.

questions.prompt: For `int[][] grid`, `grid[1]` is itself an array.
questions.explanation: A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays. Therefore, `grid[1]` refers to a row, while `grid[1][2]` refers to a single `int`.

questions.prompt: What does a for loop group together inside its parentheses?

options.text: Declaration, string comparison, and array copy

questions.explanation: The for loop combines `init`, `cond`, and `upd` into a readable index-based loop.

questions.prompt:
Which description matches this control-flow diagram?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    I["init"] --> C{"cond"}
    C -- yes --> B["body"] --> U["update"] --> C
    C -- no --> N["next statement"]
```

options.text: Execution of a variable declaration without a loop
Unconditional jump to the start of the program

questions.explanation: The diagram shows initialization, test, body, update, and the transition to the next statement. This is exactly the order of a for loop.
First, because `30 < 20` is false, `x` becomes 10. Then, because `10 < 20`, `y` becomes 10; the loop now ends and `x` is 10.

questions.prompt:
Which node is reached again after either of the two possible assignments?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S([Start]) --> R1["x = readInt();"] --> R2["y = readInt();"] --> C1{"x != y"}
    C1 -- yes --> C2{"x < y"}
    C2 -- yes --> A1["y = y - x;"] --> C1
    C2 -- no --> A2["x = x - y;"] --> C1
    C1 -- no --> W["write(x);"] --> E([Stop])
```
questions.explanation: Both assignments make up the loop body and then lead back to the test `x != y`, that is, to node `C1`.

questions.prompt:
What does this code output?

```java
write("sum: " + 2 + 3);
```
questions.explanation: Once the left operand is a string, the next operand is converted to text. Evaluating from left to right first produces `sum: 2`, and then `sum: 23`.

questions.prompt:
What does this code output?

```java
write("sum: " + (2 + 3));
```
questions.explanation: The parentheses force the numeric addition `2 + 3 = 5` to happen first. Only then is the result concatenated with the string.
Initially, the array contains 0 at every index. The assignment changes `a[1]` to 7, and that is the element that is output.
For a length of 3, only indices 0, 1, and 2 are valid. The runtime check detects `a[3]` as invalid.
`b = a` copies only the reference. Both variables point to the same array, so the change made through `b` is also visible through `a`.
`grid[1][2]` refers to row 1 and column 2 within that row. The value 7 is stored there and then read.
`i` takes the values 0, 1, and 2. The elements are therefore accessed in array order: 4, then 1, then 6.

questions.prompt: An array `a` of length 4 is read from left to right using the loop shown. Before each test of `i < a.length`, the first ___ elements have already been read.

context.caption: Each call to `readInt()` returns an integer. The loop reads the array starting at index 0.

questions.explanation: The loop starts with `i = 0`. Before each test, the positions from 0 through `i - 1` have been read, which is exactly `i` elements. After each read, `i` is incremented by 1.

questions.prompt: Which for loop visits every element of `a` exactly once?
questions.explanation: The indices 0 through `a.length - 1` are exactly the valid array positions. Option b skips 0, c accesses `a[a.length]` at the end, and d omits index 0.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about reducibility. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Every CFG can always be translated into a structured program.
Every MiniJava program has a CFG.
A reducible loop has exactly one entry point.
Conversion into a structured program is possible if and only if the CFG is reducible.
A jump into the middle of a loop is compatible with reducibility.

questions.explanation: Every MiniJava program has a CFG. The converse holds only for reducible graphs; multiple entry points or jumps into the middle violate this condition.

questions.prompt: Why is the edge after the body different for an `if` and a `while`?

options.text: For an `if`, it always goes to Start; for a `while`, it goes to Stop.
An `if` has no condition, while a `while` has two.
For an `if`, it goes to the next statement; for a `while`, it goes back to the condition.
For an `if`, it goes back to the body; for a `while`, it goes to the next statement.

questions.explanation: Both constructs have a test and a branch. Only the edge after the body differs: it determines whether there is a one-time choice or a repeated test.

questions.prompt: A CFG path alone completely determines the execution, even if the variable values at a branch node are unknown.
questions.explanation: At a branch node, the current variable state determines which edge is taken. That is why the state carried along is part of the operational semantics.
The loop sets the values to 2, 3, 4, and 5 at indices 0 through 3. Therefore, `a[3]` is 5.

questions.prompt:
Which while loop is equivalent to the following for loop?

```java
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; ++i) write(a[i]);
```

options.text: `{ int i = 0; while (i <= a.length) { write(a[i]); i = i + 1; } }`
`{ int i = 1; while (i <= a.length) { write(a[i]); i = i + 1; } }`
`{ int i = 0; while (i < a.length) { write(a[i]); i = i + 1; } }`
`{ int i = 0; while (i < a.length) { i = i + 1; write(a[i]); } }`

questions.explanation: The initialization comes before the loop, the body comes before the update, and then the next test takes place. The other options move the update or use an incorrect bound.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about creating arrays. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The elements of a new `int` array are initially 0.
A new `int` array is initially filled with 1.
If the variable holding the length changes later, the array grows with it.
`new int[3]` creates an array of length 3.
An array's length remains fixed after creation.

questions.explanation: The length can be determined at runtime, but is immutable afterward. New `int` elements start at 0.
`equals` compares contents. Both strings contain the same characters, so the result is `true`.
The array contains 0, 1, and 2. The minimum-finding loop starts with `a[0]` and finds no smaller value, so `result` remains 0.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about references. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `b = a` automatically creates a second array of the same size.
The variable directly stores all the array elements instead of a reference.
After `b = a`, `a` and `b` point to the same array.
A change made through `b` may be visible through `a`.

questions.explanation: The assignment copies only the reference. Therefore, both variables share the same array; no new array is created.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a two-dimensional array follows from `int[][] grid = new int[3][4]`?

options.text: There are 3 rows with 4 columns each.
Every row must retain the same length as every other row.
There are 4 rows with 3 columns each.

questions.explanation: The outer length 3 represents the rows, and the inner length 4 represents the columns. `grid[1]` is itself a row, and therefore an array.

questions.prompt:
Which edge in the diagram shows a loop's return edge?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    I["init"] --> C{"cond"}
    C -- yes --> B["body"] --> U["update"] --> C
    C -- no --> N["next statement"]
```
questions.explanation: After the body, the update step leads back to the condition test. This allows the loop to run again.
The execution first gives `x = 10`, then `y = 10`. The loop then ends, and `x = 10` is output.

questions.prompt: An array `a` of length 3 is read using the loop shown. Each call to `readInt()` returns an integer. Select all statements that apply to this loop.

context.caption: The array length is 3. Each call to `readInt()` returns an integer.

options.text: The loop reads the same elements again indefinitely.
Before each test of the loop condition, exactly `i` elements have been read.
The procedure starts with `i = 1` so that index 0 is skipped.
Each loop iteration reads one element and increments `i` by 1.
The condition `i < a.length` prevents the loop from reading `a[a.length]`.

questions.explanation: `i` starts at 0 and increases by 1 after each element is read. Thus, every valid index is read once. When `i == a.length`, the condition is false and the loop body no longer executes. Before each test, exactly `i` elements have been read.

options.text: `int i = 0; while (i <= a.length) { if (a[i] < result) result = a[i]; i = i + 1; }`
`int i = 1; while (i <= a.length) { if (a[i] < result) result = a[i]; i = i + 1; }`
`int i = 1; while (i < a.length) { i = i + 1; if (a[i] < result) result = a[i]; }`
`int i = 1; while (i < a.length) { if (a[i] < result) result = a[i]; i = i + 1; }`

questions.explanation: The for loop starts at 1, tests `i < a.length` before the body, and increments only after the body. Option a does exactly that.

questions.prompt: Which two values does the code output? `write(wert)` outputs the value on its own line. For `+`, as soon as one operand is a string, the other operand is converted to text; evaluation proceeds from left to right.

context.caption: The code makes two calls to `write`.

questions.explanation: In the first expression, concatenation proceeds from left to right: `s + 1` gives `x1`, then `x1 + 2` gives the text `x12`. In the second line, the parentheses are evaluated first: `1 + 2` gives 3, so `x3` is output.

questions.prompt: The following minimum-finding algorithm first sets `result` to `a[0]` and starts the loop at `i = 1`. The array has at least one element. What role does this initialization play in the algorithm?

context.caption: The algorithm outputs the minimum of the nonempty array.

options.text: Before the first loop test, it provides a value that is the minimum of the elements considered so far.
It ensures that index 0 is deliberately never considered.
It ensures that the loop starts at `i = 0` and reads `a[-1]`.
It ensures that the array length remains variable.

questions.explanation: Before the first loop test, only `a[0]` has been considered. With `result = a[0]`, `result` is already the minimum of the range considered so far. The loop then checks the elements starting at index 1.

questions.prompt:
Which property distinguishes the two subgraphs?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph reduzierbar
    S1([Start]) --> L1((loop)) --> X1(( )) --> L1
    X1 --> E1([Stop])
    end
    subgraph nicht_reduzierbar
    S2([Start]) --> L2((loop)) --> X2(( )) --> L2
    S2 --> X2
    X2 --> E2([Stop])
    end
```

options.text: The loop on the left has two independent entry points.
The loop on the right has no Stop node.
The loop on the right has an additional entry into its middle.
The loop on the left has no return edge at all.

questions.explanation: In the non-reducible subgraph, in addition to the edge from `L2`, there is a path directly from `S2` to `X2`. The loop therefore has more than one entry point.
`grid[0]` remains the original row with value 4 at index 1. `grid[1]` can be made to refer to a new row, which then has length 1.
`result` starts at 5, is replaced when compared with 2, and remains unchanged when compared with 7. The minimum is therefore 2.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about for loops and their execution order. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The execution order is still init, test, body, update, next test.
Transforming a for loop into a while loop can make the structure of the individual steps visible.
The body runs even if the first test evaluates to false.
In the source code, `init`, `cond`, and `upd` are grouped together inside the for-loop parentheses.
The update expression runs before the first test.

questions.explanation: The for syntax groups the three parts, but semantically the first test comes before the body and update. If it is false, the body is skipped; the while-loop transformation makes this order explicit.

questions.prompt: A single pass through an array with $n$ elements checks each element exactly once. Which runtime class applies?
questions.explanation: The number of checks grows in proportion to the number of elements. This corresponds to $\Theta(n)$, as in a single pass through a sorted list.

options.text: `x < y`; it outputs immediately afterward every time.
`x == 0`; the variables are subtracted down to 0.
`x > y`; this test terminates the loop.
`x == y`; for positive values, the subtractions eventually lead to this.

questions.explanation: The loop test is `x != y`, so the loop ends when the values are equal. With positive inputs, the values remain positive, and the Euclidean algorithm eventually reaches the case `x = y`.

questions.prompt: Your navigation app calculates a route. The program has a branch depending on the GPS signal and repeats while the destination has not been reached. Which representation models the control flow so that possible executions can be described as paths?

options.text: A two-dimensional array for map tiles

questions.explanation: A CFG models a program's control flow using nodes and edges. Each possible execution corresponds to a path through the graph.

questions.prompt: In a ticketing app, you build the display `"Platz: " + platznummer`. Which concept are you using?
questions.explanation: The `+` operator concatenates a string with the value of `platznummer`. If one operand is a string, the other value is represented as text for the concatenation.

questions.prompt: You create `int[] werte = new int[37]`. How many distinct index values are valid?
questions.explanation: For a length $n$, the valid indices range from $0$ to $n-1$. For $n=37$, that is $0$ through $36$, or $37$ indices in total.

questions.prompt: A messaging app should respond only when the entered text exactly matches `"STOP"`. Which Java check is semantically correct?
questions.explanation: `equals` compares string contents; calling it on the constant string is also safe if `eingabe` has the value `null`. `==` compares references; length or prefix alone is not enough for exact equality.

questions.prompt: A Sudoku app stores a board with 9 rows and 9 columns and should access cells directly using `feld[zeile][spalte]`. Which concept fits?
questions.explanation: A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays: `feld[zeile]` selects a row, and `[spalte]` selects an element within it. This lets you address each Sudoku cell directly.

questions.prompt: You observe the loop body: `for (int i = 3; i < 100; i += 7) { ... }`. How many times does it run?
questions.explanation: The values of `i` are $3,10,17,\ldots,94$—these are $14$ values. The update runs after each body and before the next condition test.

questions.prompt: In an image editor, you write `int[] original = new int[3]; int[] preview = original;`. Then you change `preview[1]`, and `original[1]` changes too. What explains this?

options.text: Both variables store a reference to the same array.
Java automatically creates a deep copy on every assignment.
String comparison with `equals` links the arrays.
Local variables are automatically initialized when read.

questions.explanation: An array variable contains a reference. `preview = original` does not create a new array, so both variables refer to the same object and see the same change.

questions.prompt: A scheduling app stores five weekdays as rows containing $3$, $7$, $4$, $0$, and $6$ entries, respectively. How many values are there in total in the two-dimensional array?
questions.explanation: Add the row lengths: $3+7+4+0+6=20$. A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays, so its rows may have different lengths—a length of $0$ is also possible.

questions.prompt: Is this correct: The compiler can reject `int tickets; System.out.println(tickets);` even though `tickets` might later contain `0`, because local variables have no default value.
questions.explanation: Local variables are not initialized automatically. Java therefore requires an assignment before the variable is first read.

questions.prompt: You want to pave a rectangular garden measuring $84\,m \times 60\,m$ with the largest possible square slabs and no waste. Which cases typically use the same core of the Euclidean algorithm?

options.text: Reducing a fraction using the greatest common divisor of its numerator and denominator.
Checking whether two chat messages have the same content.
Finding the largest possible square slab size for the rectangle.
Storing a table with rows of different lengths.

questions.explanation: The Euclidean algorithm computes the greatest common divisor, for example to find the square slab size or to reduce a fraction. String contents are compared with `equals`, while rows of different lengths are a property of two-dimensional arrays.
